title: The unknown god (Acts 17:16–34)
hook: Paul notices an altar to an unknown god and starts from there
tomorrow: a gifted preacher gets it partly wrong. who corrects him, and where?

segments.voice: The Bereans heard gladly, then searched daily. Now Paul is in Athens on his own, and the people listening don't share his scriptures at all.

A family dinner, and across the table sits someone whose faith, or lack of one, is miles from yours. Where do you even start? Paul has that dinner with a whole city. In Athens, waiting for his friends, Acts says "his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry." Some philosophers call him a babbler and bring him up to the Areopagus, Mars' hill, to explain himself. Here's his chance to say everything that bothered him. Instead, he starts with an altar he passed on his walk, an altar with no name on it.
screen: `ACROSS THE TABLE, MILES APART.` → `HIS SPIRIT WAS STIRRED.` → `HE STARTS WITH THEIR ALTAR.`

segments.voice: His opening line: "For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you." Their altar, their reaching, is his first step. Then he builds outward. God, he says, "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." That's the one to tell a friend tonight: before Paul says anything that divides the hill, he says what everyone on it shares. One blood. Every nation. And God made people to look for him, "if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us." Feel after him: like a hand reaching in a dark room. Then Paul borrows from their shelf, not his, and quotes their own poets: "For we are also his offspring." Only after all that does he speak of a man God raised from the dead, and that's where the hill divides. "Some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter." A few stay, and Acts names two of them, Dionysius and a woman called Damaris. So what does this give you for a hard conversation this week? Start where the other person already stands. Honor what's true there. Then say what you came to say.
screen: `TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` · `ONE BLOOD, ALL NATIONS.` · `THEIR OWN POETS.` · `SOME MOCKED; SOME STAYED.` · then, large: `NOT FAR FROM EACH ONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose views sit far from yours. The wish: one good conversation with them. The obstacle: the thing you'd be tempted to lead with. The plan: name one thing they honestly care about, something you could honor without pretending, and decide that's where you'll start.
The unknown god. An altar in Athens with no name on it, and the place Paul chose to begin.
Your line: not far from each one. Paul said it to a crowd that didn't share his faith. Go well.

howItsDone: Christians read Acts 17 in church and in Bible study, and some look to Paul's words on Mars' hill when they talk about faith with people who see the world differently.

fork.setup: your new coworker isn't religious, and she volunteers every Saturday at an animal shelter. she asks what your faith is even about. what's a Mars' hill way to start?
options: start from what she already loves: caring for the helpless.
start by listing what her life is missing without God.
start with the resurrection; it's the heart of the faith.
fork.reveal: Paul began with their altar and their poets, and came to the resurrection last. he started where his listeners already stood.

what it means: an altar in Athens with no name, and Paul's starting point: him declare I unto you.
what a scholar hears: Paul builds his speech from their altar, one blood for all nations, and their poets before he ever names the resurrection, and that's where the hill divides.
guess: an Athens altar where Paul chose to begin
a hidden god only philosophers knew
a god Paul invented to win the crowd

Areopagus.meaning: a hill in Athens, also called Mars' hill, where Paul spoke

idolatry.meaning: worship of carved images or gods

Dionysius.meaning: a man on Mars' hill who believed

Damaris.meaning: a woman Acts names among those who believed

notes: The index carry 'not far from each one' paraphrases the KJV's 'not far from every one of us' (Acts 17:27); the teach quotes the KJV. Kept the index carry as required.
Acts 17:28 credits 'For we are also his offspring' to 'your own poets'; the lesson names no poet (scholars often point to Aratus) under the claims rule.
KJV 'THE UNKNOWN GOD'; the Greek has no article and many readers translate 'to an unknown god'. Left out of the spoken text; a scholar may want it in the trapdoor.
The babbler question (Acts 17:18) comes from 'certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks'; the hook says 'some philosophers'. Confirm.

Unity thread (owner, 'one human race'): Acts 17:26 'hath made of one blood all nations of men' is quoted and named as the one-to-tell-a-friend detail: Paul says what every listener shares before what divides them. This is Paul's own claim in the text, given as such; it does not say all religions are the same. Confirm the framing.
